haiku-low.q1: MySQL first, then Postgres, in the write path. If the Postgres part fails or times out, the user still gets success. The pending row stays for the sweeper.
haiku-low.q2: Only if the existing row's version is lower than the incoming version. A missing row is simply inserted. Equal or higher existing versions are never overwritten.
haiku-low.q3: Every instance must run the new code, and app_flag_value{flag="users.write_mode"} must show dual_mysql_primary on all of them. Instances can disagree for up to 30 seconds.
haiku-low.q4: It reads the replica in primary-key order, 2,000 rows per batch. It waits 10 seconds whenever mysql_replica_lag_seconds is above 5.
haiku-low.q5: Reads move through the ramp only with hourly holds, fallback under 0.1%, p99 at most 1.5x MySQL, and a clean comparer. Reaching 100% needs 3 days and a clean pass. The brief does not give separate source-of-truth prerequisites beyond the checklist.
haiku-low.q6: A pending row, committed in the same transaction as the write, in the primary database's user_sync_pending table. The sweeper copies the user to the secondary and removes the row if its token is unchanged.
haiku-low.q7: Every copy and delete of a user takes the per-user lock, so they never overlap. Delete adds a tombstone in the same secondary transaction, and copies skip tombstoned ids.
haiku-low.q8: Progress is in the one-row backfill_progress table, holding last_id. Each batch's copies and last_id update share one Postgres transaction. The brief does not state where the backfill stops.
haiku-low.q9: The comparer walks both tables in id order and rechecks mismatches against the primaries after 30 seconds. Confirmed ones get a pending row, are counted in users_compare_mismatches, and the sweeper repairs them.
haiku-low.q10: Writes pause up to 90 seconds, and one flag change sets the new mode and clears the pause, issued within 60 seconds. If any wait runs out, the switch aborts, clears the pause, and keeps the mode.
haiku-low.q11: Postgres assigns ids after the switch, from its sequence set to max(highest MySQL id, highest tombstone id) plus 1,000,000. On rollback, MySQL receives rows with explicit ids and its auto-increment moves past them.
haiku-low.q12: MySQL stays a secondary receiving every write via pending rows and the sweeper for 14 days. Rollback runs the switch script with dual_mysql_primary and read_from_pg 0, pausing writes up to 90 seconds. It ends at step 9, when write_mode becomes pg_only.

sonnet.q1: MySQL first (in one transaction with a pending row), then after commit Postgres (dual_mysql_primary, 1 second timeout). If Postgres fails or times out, it is logged and the caller still sees success; the pending row stays for the sweeper.
sonnet.q2: Only if the row is missing (insert) or the existing row's version is lower than the incoming version (ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE ... WHERE users.version < EXCLUDED.version). Deletes are handled separately. Copies are also skipped if the id has a tombstone.
sonnet.q3: Every instance must run the new code and app_flag_value{flag="users.write_mode"} must show dual_mysql_primary on all of them. Instances refresh flags every 30 seconds, so they can disagree for up to 30 seconds.
sonnet.q4: It reads the replica (not the primary) in primary-key order in batches of 2,000 rows, and waits 10 seconds whenever mysql_replica_lag_seconds is above 5 (reporting jobs share the replica).
sonnet.q5: Reads move after: tables created, new code deployed, dual writes on, backfill done, and a full comparer pass clean. Ramp 1, 10, 50, 100%, holding each step at least 1 hour, continuing only if fallback rate is under 0.1%, Postgres read p99 is at most 1.5x MySQL's, and the comparer is still clean; at 100% hold at least 3 days with the latest comparer pass clean. The switch (step 7) comes after that: the switch script's steps must complete: pause set and seen by every instance, plus 10 seconds wait, pending table of the current primary empty, id sequence set, all within the time budget.
sonnet.q6: A row in the pending table (user_sync_pending), with a random token, for that user id. It is kept in the primary database (MySQL here), written in the same transaction as the write. The sweeper (a loop in a worker process) copies the user to Postgres using the version rule, then removes the pending row if its token is unchanged.
sonnet.q7: Tombstones in user_tombstones (in the secondary database) plus the per-user lock. A copy is skipped if the id has a tombstone. A delete takes the lock, then adds the tombstone and removes the row in one secondary transaction; since copies take the same lock, a copy cannot slip in between a delete and its tombstone.
sonnet.q8: In the one-row Postgres table backfill_progress (last_id, the last id of the last completed batch). Each batch is a single Postgres transaction that copies the rows and sets last_id, so they commit together. A crash resumes after last_id. NOT STATED where it stops (the end condition is not given beyond copying the existing ~38 million rows).
sonnet.q9: The comparer: it walks the MySQL replica and Postgres in id order, 2,000 rows at a time, comparing every column. It rechecks each mismatch against the primaries after 30 seconds; if still there, it adds a pending row for that id and counts it in users_compare_mismatches, and the sweeper repairs it. A Postgres row with a tombstone also counts as a mismatch.
sonnet.q10: Writes are paused with users.write_paused_until (retryable 503s) so no writes happen while instances may disagree; wait for all instances to report the pause, then 10 more seconds, drain pending, then change write_mode and clear the pause in one atomic flag change (flags change as a set). If a wait runs out or step 4 cannot be issued within 60 seconds of step 1, the script aborts: it clears the pause and leaves write_mode unchanged. Pause is at most 90 seconds, and expires by itself at its deadline if the script crashes.
sonnet.q11: The Postgres id sequence assigns ids after the switch (MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT before). At the switch it is set to the larger of (highest users.id in MySQL, highest tombstone id) plus 1,000,000, so ids are not reused and do not collide with tombstones. On rollback, MySQL receives those rows with explicit ids and its auto-increment moves past them.
sonnet.q12: MySQL becomes the secondary and gets every write via the same pending-row and sweeper mechanism with roles swapped. Rollback: run the switch script with write_mode = dual_mysql_primary and read_from_pg = 0 (writes pause at most 90 seconds, no write lost). The option ends at step 9 (write_mode = pg_only), no sooner than 14 days after the switch, after which rollback is no longer possible and MySQL users is backed up and dropped.
